title: We Celebrate Invented Spelling. Why Don't We Extend That Thinking to Mathematics?
author: AubreeTeaches
summary: Early childhood educators routinely celebrate 'invented spelling' — children's phonetic approximations like 'SED' for 'said' — as evidence of phonemic awareness and developmental thinking rather than errors. Yet when children use invented or informal strategies in mathematics (counting on fingers, drawing arrays, using partial products), these are often corrected toward standard algorithms too quickly, treating the child's reasoning as something to be replaced rather than built upon. The author argues that the same developmental respect extended to early literacy should govern mathematics instruction: unconventional strategies reveal a child's conceptual understanding of quantity, place value, and structure. Forcing early transitions to standard procedures often bypasses the conceptual stage entirely, producing procedural fluency without understanding. Educators should instead honor children's mathematical representations — concrete models, invented procedures, partial strategies — as legitimate and intellectually valuable, recognizing that all of these are moves toward, not away from, mathematical maturity.
points: Invented spelling is celebrated as evidence of developmental phonemic awareness — the same framework should apply to children's invented mathematical strategies, which reveal genuine conceptual understanding of number, quantity, and operation.

Rushing children from informal mathematical strategies to standard algorithms bypasses the conceptual stage that gives procedures meaning; students gain procedural fluency without the structural understanding that makes it flexible and durable.

Concrete models and representations in math are not pre-mathematical crutches — they are the conceptual scaffolding through which abstract relationships become accessible, and honoring them is honoring cognition.

The distinction between 'errors to fix' and 'thinking to build upon' is a pedagogical stance with profound effects: treating children's strategies as windows into understanding changes the teacher's role from corrector to interpreter.

Consistency of principle matters across subject areas: an early childhood educator who celebrates invented spelling but penalizes invented mathematical strategies is applying an inconsistent theory of learning and development.
quotes: A child writes 'SED' instead of said. We celebrate this. We understand this child is using what they know about sounds to make meaning. We understand this is evidence of phonemic awareness, of a developing understanding of how letters and sounds work together.
When we honor children's early mathematical strategies, concrete models, and representations, we're recognizing the very same truth.

The rush to standard algorithms can rob children of the opportunity to develop the conceptual understanding that gives those algorithms meaning. We want automaticity, yes. But we want understanding before automaticity.
